explanation:
## Battery Runtime Fundamentals

Battery runtime is a core calculation in electronics, portable device design, and DIY projects. Dividing the battery's capacity (in milliamp-hours, mAh) by the device's average current draw (in milliamps, mA) gives you the estimated operating time in hours.

---

## How It's Calculated

The base formula is:

**Runtime (hours) = Battery capacity (mAh) ÷ Current draw (mA)**

**Direct example:** A 3,000 mAh battery powering an ESP32 actively transmitting over Wi-Fi (≈150 mA average):
3,000 ÷ 150 = **20 theoretical hours**

With real-world efficiency losses (~80%), practical runtime would be roughly **16 hours**.

> **Why the unit works:** 1 mAh = the charge delivered by 1 mA sustained for 1 hour. The division cancels the units correctly: mAh ÷ mA = h.

---

## Correcting for Real-World Efficiency

The theoretical result is always optimistic. Batteries never deliver 100% of their rated capacity, for several concrete reasons:

| Factor | Typical loss |
|---|---|
| DC-DC conversion (boost/buck) | 5–15% |
| Heat generated by the battery | 5–10% |
| Cutoff voltage (the battery doesn't discharge to 0 V) | 10–20% |
| Cell aging (charge cycles) | an additional 5–20% over time |
| Low temperature (<10 °C) | up to 30% less effective capacity |

**Recommended efficiency factor for estimates:** multiply the result by **0.7–0.85** depending on the system. Commercial power banks typically operate at 70–80% real-world efficiency, since they include protection circuits and voltage conversion.

---

## Typical Current Draw by Device

If you don't know your device's exact draw, these ranges are a starting point. Consumption varies with screen brightness, active radios (Wi-Fi, BT, LTE), and processing load.

| Device / component | Typical draw |
|---|---|
| BLE sensor (idle / sleep mode) | 0.01–1 mA |
| Arduino Uno (active, no peripherals) | 40–50 mA |
| ESP32 / Wi-Fi microcontroller (active) | 80–250 mA |
| Wireless earbuds (per bud) | 5–15 mA |
| LED strip (per meter, medium brightness) | 200–600 mA |
| Smartphone (screen on, browsing) | 200–400 mA |
| Smartphone (gaming / video streaming) | 600–1,500 mA |
| Tablet in active use | 500–1,000 mA |
| Small DC motor / fan | 100–500 mA |
| Raspberry Pi 4 (idle → full load) | 600–1,300 mA |
| Action camera (4K recording) | 900–1,400 mA |

**Where to find the exact figure:** look up the manufacturer's specifications under "typical current consumption," or measure directly with a multimeter in series or a USB meter such as the UM25C.

---

## Worked Example

A 10,000 mAh power bank charging a phone that draws 800 mA on average:

- **Theoretical:** 10,000 ÷ 800 = 12.5 hours
- **Real (75% efficiency):** ≈ 9.4 hours of effective charging

Power banks lose energy converting the lithium cells' internal 3.7 V to the 5 V USB output, plus losses in the cable and the phone's own charging circuit.

---

## What This Calculation Does NOT Include

This model assumes **constant draw**, a useful simplification with clear limits:

- **It doesn't account for variable consumption:** a smartphone alternates between screen-on (300 mA), standby (5–15 mA), and push notifications. Real consumption is a weighted average.
- **It doesn't model the battery's discharge curve:** lithium-ion batteries hold a stable voltage down to ~20% charge and then drop sharply. This can affect voltage-sensitive devices before the actual charge runs out.
- **It doesn't apply to systems with pass-through charging:** efficiency degrades further.
- **It doesn't predict battery lifespan in cycles:** that requires the manufacturer's capacity-per-cycle data (typically 300–500 cycles to 80% of original capacity for standard Li-ion, per IEC 61960).

---

## Common Mistakes

**1. Confusing mAh with mA:** Capacity (mAh) and draw (mA) are different quantities. Dividing mAh by mAh makes no physical sense.

**2. Using peak draw instead of the average:** Peak current (for example, when a motor starts) can be 3–5× the steady-state draw. For runtime, what matters is the **sustained average draw**.

**3. Ignoring self-discharge:** Lithium batteries lose ~1–3% of their charge per month in storage. Relevant if the device sits unused between sessions.

**4. Assuming more mAh is always better:** At equal chemistry and voltage, yes. But comparing a 3.7 V Li-ion battery with a 3.2 V LiFePO4 of equal mAh gives different energies (Wh = V × Ah). To compare across chemistries, use **Wh as the unit**.

faq.q: How long will my phone battery last with this calculator?
faq.a: Find your battery capacity in phone settings and estimate average current draw. Light use: 100–150 mA, moderate use: 200–300 mA, gaming or video: 400+ mA. The result is theoretical maximum under constant load.

faq.q: What's the difference between mAh and Wh?
faq.a: Wh (watt-hours) = (mAh × Voltage) ÷ 1000. Wh is a more accurate measure of total energy stored, while mAh describes capacity at a specific voltage (usually 3.7V for lithium cells).

faq.q: Why does my actual battery life fall short of this estimate?
faq.a: Real devices have highly variable power draw. Idle consumption is much lower than active use. Screen brightness, cellular radios, Wi-Fi, GPS, and background apps all increase draw above the average.

faq.q: How many charge cycles do lithium batteries last?
faq.a: Most lithium batteries tolerate 300–1000 charge cycles (typically 500–800) before capacity drops to ~80%. This varies by chemistry, thermal conditions, and charging practices.

faq.q: Does fast charging reduce battery lifespan?
faq.a: Yes. Fast charging generates significant heat, which stresses battery chemistry. Charging between 20% and 80%, avoiding fast charging, and keeping devices cool extend lifespan dramatically.

faq.q: How does temperature affect battery runtime and health?
faq.a: Cold reduces runtime by 15–30% but doesn't cause permanent damage. Heat (above 95°F) accelerates degradation. Optimal performance is 68–72°F. Avoid freezing or overheating your device.

faq.q: What's the best charge level for battery longevity?
faq.a: Keeping charge between 20% and 80% significantly extends battery lifespan compared to 0–100% cycles. Many modern phones have optional battery health features that cap charging at 80%.

faq.q: Is this calculator reliable for my device?
faq.a: It's reliable for steady-state estimates under constant load. Real devices alternate between idle, moderate, and peak power draw. Use this as a theoretical maximum; expect actual runtime 20–40% shorter with mixed usage.
